speakeroldname: Mr. Simon de Jong (Regina East) moved:
speechtext:
That a Royal Commission of Inquiry be created to study the nuclear fuel cycle in Canada including the range of economic, social, medical, environmental and safety matters resulting from exploration, mining, production, transportation, storage and use of uranium and its byproducts.
He said: Mr. Speaker, today my Party, the New Democratic Party, has introduced this motion during its Opposition Day. We feel the time is long overdue for the public of Canada to be afforded an opportunity to look at the Canadian nuclear industry, from the mining aspect to the enrichment, to the use and export and sale of uranium and nuclear reactors.
There is no doubt that the introduction of nuclear energy, brought about by some important and historic discoveries by Albert Einstein and many other prominent scientists, has opened up a whole new vista for the world, namely a new energy which was originally touted to be the great saviour and a solution to many human problems by providing an endless supply of energy. What we have found is that while the potential of this new energy has not been fully realized, many of its dangers are more than apparent to us today. This new energy has placed the world on the brink of its own selfdestruction through nuclear weaponry. The threat of devastating and destroying large sections of our environment is yet another danger that arises out of this new discovery, nuclear energy.
Just to give you some example of the scale with which we are dealing, Mr. Speaker, the half life of uranium and other radioactive particles is measured in thousands of years. A mistake, then, is a thousand-year mistake. An environmental mistake can destroy hundreds and thousands of acres or miles, which destruction will last for thousands of years, longer than the existence of the pyramids.
Dealing with an energy that is so potent, the effects of which can be felt for such a long time, requires a tremendous sense of social responsibility by the institutions that deal with it. They are the scientific community, government and industry. What we have seen, in fact, is social irresponsibility by the handlers of the nuclear industry. In my own province, when my Party was in power it decided to go ahead with the development of uranium mines in northern Saskatchewan. At that time, publicly and within the Party conventions, I opposed that move. One of my reasons was that while the Party was in power it could take all the necessary safeguards and precautions to make certain that the environment and the safety and health of workers is not in danger; but the time could come when
another party would be in power which would not have the same regard for the health and safety of the workers and the environment.
[DOT]	0115)
The events of the last few weeks have demonstrated the social irresponsibility of the Saskatchewan Conservative Government. Since taking office it has drastically reduced the monitoring capacity of the provincial government. For example, in its budget of March, 1982 it cut the program that deals with occupational health and safety by 14 per cent in funds and by 17 per cent in staff. Since taking office it has also cut the budget of its Department of the Environment by some 18 per cent. It has chopped 11 per cent of the Department's budget and 20 per cent of its staff. This is the Department that is responsible for making sure that the environment of northern Saskatchewan is not in danger.
The budget for the mines pollution control branch that is supposed to monitor the work in uranium mines was cut by 39 per cent and the staff was cut by 42 per cent. This is a case of a government anxious to reduce its deficit, anxious to get the revenues from the uranium mines onstream as fast as possible, and for that it is willing to take certain risks and cut certain corners. The end result is the most major environment accident-and I put "accident" in quotation marks, Mr. Speaker-in Saskatchewan's history with over 100 million litres of radioactive water now loose in that environment.
Can we honestly say that the federal Government has dealt with the uranium question in a responsible manner? Thanks to Canada's contribution by selling the Candu reactor to India, India now has a nuclear bomb. Canada has sold Candu technology to Pakistan and it will soon have the first Muslim bomb. We are quite anxious to sell Candu reactors to Argentina, South Korea and Romania. What great democracies these are with a tremendous history of social responsibility!
I charge the Government with total irresponsibility, not only to Canadian citizens but to citizens of the world, by merchandising technology that would allow the creation of nuclear devices and nuclear bombs by people with a history of nuclear irresponsibility. Certainly they do not have a history of democracy.
I should like to deal with the economic question now. Does the nuclear industry make any economic sense? So far in this country I understand that the nuclear industry has been subsidized by up to $4 billion. It is a very expensive form of energy that requires 40 per cent subsidization. That just does not make any economic sense. The citizens of Ontario will be paying billions of dollars, for years to come, Mr. Speaker, for their nuclear power plants, many of which cannot be used. Many of them are out of commission. Heavy water plants, Mr. Speaker, were over-built. They now have to be taken apart at a cost, again, of hundreds of millions of dollars.
[DOT]	(1120)
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the great planners in the energy sector, particularly when it comes to nuclear energy, have
January 23, 1984

made some horrendous mistakes which are going to cost the average citizens of Canada hundreds of millions of dollars in the years ahead. Yet the Government is not willing to call a halt to these fantastic sums of money being poured down the drain. It is not willing to say: "Enough is enough; we have made a mistake. Let us cut our losses and look for some alternatives". The economics just do not make sense on a public level.
There are those who propose nuclear energy as a saviour for Third World countries, which need this endless source of cheap electricity. But it is not cheap, Mr. Speaker, it is very expensive, and most Third World countries cannot afford the massive loans necessary to build reactors and to create an infrastructure which would use that electricity. There are technical problems involved. For example, just out of uranium mining alone, there are 99.3 million tonnes of radioactive tailings which have to be stored in Ontario, some 20 million tonnes of such substances in Saskatchewan and 1.1 million tonnes in the Northwest Territories. Altogether there are 120 million tonnes of radioactive tailings covering 87,400 acres which Canada does not know how to dispose of properly. The 100 million tonnes of tailings in Ontario is in the Elliot Lake region. This is enough to cover a two-lane highway to a depth of three feet from Vancouver to Halifax. The problem will get worse, to quote a government document.
We do have some major technical problems, Mr. Speaker, not only with storing the tailings but in dealing with the waste from the nuclear sites themselves. We have technical problems with the Candu reactor itself. We also have problems with our agency, the Atomic Energy Control Board, the AECB. This agency is supposed to be the monitor of the nuclear industry. Yet, Mr. Speaker, there is a tremendous conflict of interest occurring there. Most of the people responsible for the monitoring originally came from the nuclear industry itself. What that "watchdog" agency is really up to, we just do not know. However, most of us are quite suspicious of the impartiality of that agency. I place on record a quote from a memo which was sent to Environment Canada from the Chief Safety Engineer, of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. This is what Mr. Liberty Pease, the Chief Engineer, had to say, and I quote:
Not only do I see no particular obligation on the part of the present generation for the comfort of future generations, but I also think we underestimate the ingenuity of future generations to control pollution from the technologies they
devise.
It is my strong personal view, that environment regulation (including nuclear regulation) is in danger of becoming a serious overkill. Regulatory agencies are responding to public hysteria, and although the intentions are good, the effect is further to aggravate the hysteria.
This is a quote from one of the watchdogs. He considers we should not be concerned about future generations, that the future generations will take care of themselves, that they will devise the technologies to take care of the tailings and the nuclear waste. I hold that up as a prime example of social irresponsibility. If this is what the people in the watchdog agency are saying, what are the people in the nuclear industry itself saying? We want a royal commission, Mr. Speaker, to look into the alternatives. For example, the economics of
Supply
nuclear energy have never made sense to me, when one realizes that if the amount of money it would take to build a nuclear power plant was spent on conservation, more electricity would be saved than the nuclear power plant would ever produce.
There are two directions in which our western industrialized society can go. We can continue down the path that we have been following, a highly capital-intensive path, one which makes no economic or environmental sense. Alternatively, we can develop conservation and the use of alternative sources of energy. Going down the nuclear path requires tremendous capital investment, produces only a few jobs, and continues the dependence of people on financial institutions and utilities for a basic need, that of electrical energy. Conservation would allow individuals to become more self-sufficient, allow them to heat their homes in a cheaper way so that they do not have to meet those high monthly utility bills. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the rational path to follow is the one leading to energy conservation and self-sufficiency.
Those are the alternatives, Mr. Speaker. However, this Government and previous governments have chosen the capital-intensive route. Some 70 per cent of the money this Government has spent on energy research has gone to the nuclear industry, with the balance, on the whole, going to the oil industry. Precious little of it has gone to conservation, or wind-generated, solar or other forms of energy. There are alternatives and it is about time we had a government with political will and vision to realize that the nuclear route is a dead-end economically and environmentally. Where the health and safety of workers is concerned, it does not make any sense. Is it not about time we started looking at alternatives?
I urge this House to accept our motion, Mr. Speaker, our call for a public inquiry. This Government is seriously contemplating building nuclear power plants in Canada to export electricity to the U.S. in order to help our balance of payments situation. Another example of social irresponsibility. This Government has given massive subsidies to the nuclear industry. We have problems with tailings and nuclear waste. The economics of this situation no longer make sense. There are dire medical consequences flowing from exposure to radiation. Much of our uranium ends up in weaponry. The judges at Nuremberg did not accept the excuse of: "Well, if it was not us, someone else would have provided it". That is no longer an excuse, Mr. Speaker. The environmental implications of the nuclear industry are everlasting. There is a conflict of interest in the AECB.
Given all that, surely the time has come where a full public inquiry into the nuclear industry is desperately needed. Let the Canadian people decide which route we should follow. Let the Canadian people in open hearings get all the facts and figures about the real risks and benefits. Let the Canadian people make those decisions rather than having them made behind closed doors.

It is an important step, Mr. Speaker. We are living in a day and age in which major global implications are coming to a head. We have the problem of the greenhouse effect. Scientists are now saying that the consequences of the greenhouse effect are irreversible and will be felt within the next 20 years. Major social, economic and agricultural changes will have to occur on a global level. We will need new forms of energy. We will have to change how we use our energy. Necessity will force us to this position in our lifetimes. Time is running out. We need a comprehensive, open national discussion and debate regarding what type of society we want and what road we should follow.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I urge the House, and in particular I urge this Government, to allow an open public inquiry into the nuclear industry. We had an excellent committee of this House which discussed and investigated alternate forms of energy. The major recommendation of that committee was that Canada go to hydrogen economy. Yet the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources has totally ignored that recommendation. The bureaucrats in the back seem to know better. Look at the mistakes they have made which are costing this country billions of dollars. Yet they have the gall, Mr. Speaker, to say that they know better! They say that the committee of Members of Parliament was just a bunch of "feelies" and their suggestions were totally off the wall because after all they are the experts. They are some experts, Mr. Speaker, who have made decisions which are costing this country billions of dollars and are endangering our environment. Through their stupidity they are introducing nuclear reactors into the world that are endangering the safety and continuing existence of the human race. Let us have a public inquiry.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle), that this House approve the following motion:
That a Royal Commission of Inquiry be created to study the nuclear fuel cycle in Canada including the range of economic, social, medical, environmental and safety matters resulting from exploration, mining, production, transportation, storage and use of uranium and its byproducts.
Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with considerable interest to the comments made by the Hon. Member. I note that he wishes a royal commission of inquiry. I would like to ask him one or two questions in relation to the substance of his remarks.
He talks about a royal commission making an inquiry. In listening to the Hon. Member, unless my interpretation is wrong, we know his position before that inquiry would take place. He would like to see the displacement in Canada of
36.000	workers involved in the nuclear industry. Since he seems to have come to a conclusion as to what ought to be done with the industry, I hope the Hon. Member will rise in his place momentarily and tell us what he would do with
36.000	displaced workers. If he has given so much consideration to making his position on an inquiry and on the nuclear
industry known, obviously he would have 10 or 15 steps readily available to put into place to hire the 36,000 workers.
We know from reports within the New Democratic Party that their policy of the past is not in line with what is happening in Canada today. I hope, Mr. Speaker, we will not get the same rhetorical answers that we have received in the past and that the Hon. Member would be kind enough to address himself to that question.

Mr. Speaker, I will answer the question in a non-rhetorical way. It is unfortunate that the question itself was not put in a non-rhetorical way.
Of course, there has to be concern for the jobs of the 36,000 people involved in the nuclear industry. You must also ask whether $4 billion that they have continued to owe to the federal Government is not quite a high price to pay to maintain those jobs. Of course, those jobs have to be phased out and alternative jobs have to be found for those people. This Party has consistently attempted to convince the Government that when you replace industries, or as industry introduces new technologies, or whatever occurs, you do it in a humane way. You do not abruptly throw all sorts of people out of work. It is unfortunate that in a whole slew of other industries that same concern is not exhibited.
I would suggest as well that there are a lot more jobs waiting in other forms of energy. The conservation program was a good program. The CHIP program was highly successful. It created many, many more jobs than the nuclear industry created at a fraction of the cost and with much more human benefit to the average Canadian. There is an area in alternative energies that can create more jobs, that will have a greater benefit to the average Canadian and cost the Canadian taxpayer less.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to note that I am very pleased to respond to this motion on this day in particular, because as I was coming into the House of Commons I was blessed by the nuclear reaction from the heavens for the first time in a long time. The warmth and light was very welcome after approximately six weeks of winter cold and snow.
I would like to respond to the motion and the proposal by the NDP for the establishment of a royal commission to consider the nuclear industry in Canada, to elaborate on some of the specific issues and ultimately put forward some specific recommendations that have been considered by the Conservative Party.
It must be realized that regardless of a particular attitude of a political party or even a country, the use of nuclear reactions is something we have to deal with because it is here to stay. It is understood scientifically and will be dealt with scientifically. While its use as an energy source around the world will depend
Supply
very much on a number of factors, the amount of nuclear energy being produced in the world at the present time means that this source is here to stay.
France is probably the best example to prove its permanence since 50 per cent of France's electricity production is from the nuclear source. Technological breakthroughs have taken place in this industry, not without difficulty or future problems, which mean that it is an energy source with which we will be living in the future.
I was disappointed by one point in particular made by the NDP spokesman this morning. When discussing nuclear reactions he talked about two things. He discussed the nuclear fission reactions in our reactors for the purpose of producing electricity and other forms of energy, and he also talked about nuclear bombs. I suggest that is an irresponsible political reaction that is regrettable and should not be permitted to stand because closer scrutiny proves it untrue. While both the plentiful supply of energy which can be produced from the nuclear reactor and the destructive force of a nuclear bomb should be considered, there are many more uses of nuclear energy as well. I would ask the member from the NDP if he is aware that over 13 million person-years of life have been saved by cobalt.
This debate today is also interesting in light of two incidents which occurred last week. If the Hon. Member from the NDP saw The Journal on CBC last week, he will know that at the same time as it was considering the significant and serious problem of what occurred in Saskatchewan, it also reported the serious incident in Japan when over 60 lives were lost in a coal mine. These two events occurred at the same time.
The main proposal of this motion is to establish a royal commission to scrutinize the industry from one end to the other. While I am not against royal commissions, the establishment of the Macdonald Commission has not greatly encouraged me to support them. I do not know how long that commission will continue, what we can expect to achieve from it or what it will cost the Canadian public, and I am not sure in this instance whether a royal commission is the answer to considering the nuclear industry in Canada.
It is clear that there is a need for additional scrutiny of the industry in a number of ways and that the present system is unsatisfactory in a number of ways. In fact, it was on that basis that in December of 1982 I presented a Private Member's Bill which was designed to revise the Atomic Energy Control Act. What we hoped to achieve through the proposals of that legislation was the creation of a nuclear control board that was composed of people without vested interests in the nuclear industry, the establishment of a radioactive decontamination fund, to require site approval as the first step in establishing a new facility, the disclosure of unclassified documents, and to make the Minister ultimately responsible for the board report to Parliament on a regular basis. Whether these specific proposals or others are followed, it is clear that there is a need for improved scrutiny and understanding of what is happening in the industry. There have been many specific situations when I believe both the public interest and the

industry's interest would have been better served if there had been a better understanding and recognition of what was going on.
It should also be noted that there have been many problems throughout the history of the nuclear industry in Canada as a result of the Government's incompetence to deal with it through its Crown corporation, AECL, and by the actions of many Liberals throughout its history who were responsible for making export deals. The Chalk River project could have gone much further and more quickly if it had not been for some of the unfortunate interventions and actions of past Liberal Party members and Government Ministers.
Let us examine the health aspect of the nuclear industry which I believe is on the minds of most Canadians. What is the real problem in this area? In the uranium mining industry, for instance, everyone knows that the uranium mines have radioactive wastes and tailings, but what is their real significance? We know that in northern Ontario the Serpent River system has had some contamination. The effect of this contamination at its worst has been that the water in that system represented a hazard equivalent to that from smoking about one cigarette a year, assuming that people drink nothing but that water. While the hazard is not zero, I suggest that it is insignificant when compared with other hazards which we face on a daily basis. Perhaps the Hon. Member and I, who probably smoke more than one cigarette in an hour, should think about that seriously.
What about the history of the industry and its workers? I had occasion to visit the original nuclear complex in England. I have also received information from the statistics that were available from Ontario Hydro. I can say from all the statistics that exist in England that the mortality rate for workers in the nuclear industry, including those deaths caused by cancer, are less than the average death rate from cancer. It may be slightly higher in the Ontario Hydro figures, but again it is insignificant.
Three Mile Island had much publicity. What is the net effect of the accident which occurred at Three Mile Island? The best scientific judgment of the effects of the accident is that it will lead to less than one additional fatal cancer in a population of 300,000 people some time over the next 40 years. The number of fatal cancers in that population over that period from other causes is expected to be about 60,000. It was a serious accident, but relatively speaking and compared with other forms of energy-even many of the soft-path energy forms-it is a small and almost insignificant factor.
The economic impact was mentioned. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Dingwall) made a very good point, that 36,000 jobs in the nuclear industry are on the line in one way or another throughout Canada. These break down into approximately
6,000	jobs in mining, about 3,280 jobs in research and development, about 4,000 jobs in engineering and design, 6,000 jobs in manufacturing, 11,000 jobs in construction, 5,600 jobs in
operations and maintenance, and 250 jobs in public administration.
These are not jobs at which we can look in the same way as we can look at jobs in a number of other industries. These jobs are at the leading edge of technology. Without any argument at all that there should be and will be changes in the future in this type of technology, Canada is at the leading edge. The New Democratic Party is suggesting that we go back and not consider this as an opportunity but as a hazard. I suggest very strongly that in going back and denying this entire area in which Canada has always maintained a near forefront position, indeed we would lose a valuable opportunity in the future. I cannot believe that the NDP would suggest that that is the right way to go, but that is its position.
What is the future of the industry in Canada? Perhaps one of the reasons the NDP is asking for a royal commission now is that the Government has avoided dealing with the issue publicly. It had an internal discussion, one that is suspect but one that produced some results. I do not know whether it made any final decision because it had three or four options to consider. These options ranged from doing absolutely nothing and letting the industry die away-and that would be the future of the industry if there was no additional consideration in a year or so of what was happening-to the idea of having dedicated nuclear plants for the export of electricity to the United States. In between there was a range and combination of things which could be done.
It is clear that if nothing is done we will continue to have an industry which will atrophy. If we cannot export more units to places such as Taiwan, China or Turkey, and if we do not do it on a reasonable basis, we are in danger of seeing the industry die despite whether or not we continue to use nuclear reactors in Canada. I do not know what the Government has finally decided. When the Minister speaks, perhaps he will tell us. I think this is one of the reasons the NDP and others justifiably criticize the Government. No one knows what it is doing; perhaps the Government does not know what it is doing.
If we look at what is actually happening, with the number of layoffs at AECL, the number of closures and the overbuild of heavy water, questions come to mind. Perhaps the Minister could tell us how many millions of dollars worth of heavy water are continuing to be produced in Glace Bay and Port Hawkesbury and what he anticipates doing with it in the near future. The stockpile of $100 million worth of heavy water was reached two years ago. How big is the stockpile now? These questions should be answered in an open and forthright manner.
We have had many serious discussions within our Party about the nuclear industry. We have considered in some detail some of the things we could do to help with the problem. Indeed, it started in 1979 when the Government appointed a task force to consider the whole issue. I am not sure whether we have the luxury, both in terms of the industry and the technology which is at stake around the world, to not get moving. I am not sure whether we have the luxury for a task force or a royal commission. There is no question the scrutiny
January 23, 1984

it would bring would be welcome and desirable, but I think it is time for the Government to take some positive action. It cannot do it by making a deal with Yugoslavia with contra-trade agreements which will deny other industries in Canada or by selling our technology in a way that we will end up having given away our technology and all the opportunities it creates in terms of jobs and development in Canada. We cannot do it that way. We have to do it in a way which will benefit Canada in the long term. We have to do it with the confidence that nations will not exploit our technology for developing destructive forces. I am sure the Minister is very familiar with all these elements.
In the last few minutes remaining, I would like to mention some specific ideas which I think are important and can be implemented. The nuclear industry must be rationalized. Indeed, that is being done. Many times industries have had to compete against each other and certainly, for the amount of economic activity there was, it was not affordable. The industry has to rationalize itself and the Government has to rationalize itself. Historically, if we go back to the Argentinian deals or other negotiations which were very fruitless, we know there is a lot of room for increased co-operation among Government Departments and within the Crown Corporation, AECL.
We call for an open and full discussion of our waste management disposal system particularly. Having visited Whiteshell, as I am sure the Minister must have done by now, I know we have one of the best programs available anywhere in the world. Other nations are looking carefully at the results for opportunities to cure their disposal problems. We should have a full and open discussion of it to ensure that the public is aware and that we are going in a direction that is in our interests. Also we should ensure that internally our nuclear reactors are part of an overall industrial strategy. It is clear we do not have an industrial strategy. It is particularly important in this area because we have opportunities with our reactors, whether it be in Point Lepreau, Gentilly, NPD or Pickering. We have opportunities to make our nuclear resource really help in terms of industrial opportunities. Those opportunities range from using the additional energy produced from the nuclear source not just for electricity but for a whole range of industrial applications which can be of positive benefit to the economy.
In addition, Canadian energy policy-and this is one of the major failings of the NDP-has to be directed toward considering this source as an integral part of all other sources, not just as a component which can be dropped in or dropped out. It has to be considered as it is tied into the environment, to other energy sources and so on. The lack of integration of nuclear energy and nuclear research and development is a big negative in terms of the way the Government is approaching it now. I do not think I am communicating very well with the Minister, but there are not many people who are approaching nuclear energy on that basis. Whether it is hydrogen, ethanol or methanol, the nuclear reactor has a very great role to play.

Finally, we should not only develop a sound strategy for export of electricity to the United States from nuclear reactors, but we should also for our export market potential develop a strategy that will see a Candu nuclear reactor become the centre of an industrial complex for a country. Prior to the construction, design and development of these reactors, we have an opportunity that most other countries do not have in making this an energy centre rather than just a nuclear reactor for the production of electricity which is of limited value, particularly in developing countries.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your attention and for the opportunity of joining in this debate.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct just one question to my colleague from Bruce-Grey. After listening to his remarks, I would like him to tell me if the Conservative Party's policy on atomic energy development is the same as that of the Liberal Party.
Mr. Speaker, I would be delighted to answer very specifically the question that was asked of me, but that is precisely the problem. The Liberal Party of Canada has no policies.
What is yours?
That was not the question.
Mr. Speaker, I was waiting for the light.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: You need a light.

If I was waiting for a light from over there, I would have to wait a million years. The Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin), who is a physician, implied that because of the Japanese coal mine disaster more lives are lost in the non-nuclear energy field than in the nuclear field. That is quite true if you are talking about immediate disasters. However, as a physician, surely the Hon. Member is fully apprised of the long-term health hazards of working close to and with nuclear materials.
As a physician and certainly as a parliamentarian, will he comment on the long-term health hazards of the Manhattan Project at Columbia University in New York City where, after using the fissionable material, they dumped it in Buffalo? Approximately 29 to 31 years later, literally hundreds of people have died in the community where the waste material from the Manhattan Project was placed. Would the Hon. Member, both as a physician and a parliamentarian, care to comment on that?

Mr. Speaker, that is perhaps a small problem as compared to one that existed in Russia where there was a wide area that was defoliated and the entire population was injured. We can go back through history and talk about dams that have burst and thousands of lives were lost.
I would like to come back and make a comment. Can the Hon. Member tell me what consequences there will be if we do

January 23, 1984
Supply
not solve the energy needs of the world? Can he tell me the long-term consequences of carbon dioxide and the buildup in the atmosphere? If he can tell me the long-term consequences of not being able to feed the hungry of the world, I think it would be fair then for me to tell him precisely what the long-term effects of nuclear energy are going to be. I can tell him that no matter what form of energy we use on this globe, there are going to be positives and negatives. How many people die each day from the pollution that is in the atmosphere now, people with chronic bronchitis, emphysema, or heart trouble? Literally thousands are dying every day. How many people have died because of the consequences of coal mining and so on? There are positives and there are negatives.
I am not suggesting that we are stopping in a train of development here, but what is appropriate, and perhaps unfortunate in one sense, is that we can define the dangers, and we should, of nuclear wastes much more readily than we can any other waste that we know of from an energy source. That makes it a little bit easier to track. We should do that. No matter what we decide, energy will form the basis of whether we in fact in an overall way survive and are able to accomplish what we want to accomplish, not just in Canada where we have all kinds of options, which is great, but around the globe.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. With all due respect, in reply to my question, the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey asked me a question. I feel it only fair that 1 should be recognized to respond to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member does not have a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed listening to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin). He made some valid points. I especially appreciated the reasons he gave as to why we should have a public inquiry. I wish to quote from the United Kingdom Royal Commission on Environmental Pollution:
Plutonium appears to offer unique potential for threat and blackmail against society because of its great radiotoxicity and its fissile properties. The construction of a crude nuclear weapon by an illicit group is credible. We are not convinced that the government has fully appreciated the implications of this possibility.
I maintain that the same situation exists for the Canadian Government. If the Conservative Party was elected as a government and he was in charge of a nuclear program, would he and his Party approve the sale of Candu reactors to Argentina, South Korea, Taiwan, Turkey or Romania? Would they continue the same policies and sell nuclear technology that will create plutonium which, according to the U.K. study, is easily made into nuclear weaponry?

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member was here in 1979 when the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and the Conservative Party were severely criticized for our concerns with the nuclear reactor sale to Argentina and the use that clearly could be made of the materials from that reactor. I think history has proven her correct; India has been mentioned. But that is not the point. I
mentioned at the beginning of my speech, maybe in an oblique way, that the genie is out.
It is not too late to try to control the development of nuclear weapons. That is one of the most important things the world can do. However, we do not have the luxury or the option of stopping possibly 35 other countries from developing nuclear weapons, whether they use Canadian technology or not. There is no question that this Party has come out firmly, and will again, on avoiding and as far as possible limiting any involvement of Canada in the development of nuclear materials for weapons use. That goes without question. On the other hand, I do not think any of us could be so presumptuous as to assume that as Canadians we are going to stop that proliferation.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: This ends the ten-minute question and comment period.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have this occasion to participate in the debate. I have been the Minister of this Department for 17 months or more. This is really the first time that the nuclear question has been debated here or in committee when I have been present. This is a very good opportunity for me to speak on this most important topic.
The speech made by the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) on behalf of his Party is typical of the NDP. Of course, the NDP has no solution. The New Democratic Party wants to go back and forget, as the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) said, what happened 40 or 50 years ago. We now have nuclear energy available in modern society and it is not very realistic to think we can completely forget that nuclear energy ever existed. I think we have to deal on a very rational basis with the problem we have today.
The spokesman of the New Democratic Party mixed the question of nuclear weaponry with the production of Candu reactors, the production of electricity and so forth. I believe we are dealing with two different problems. I am willing to debate whether or not we should sell Candu reactors to other nations. This is a valid question. The policy of this Government and of this House is that we should not sell any part of the nuclear Candu system to any country that does not sign the international non-proliferation treaty. If a country does not sign the treaty, we do not do business with that country. We might however, decide whether or not the requirement is strict enough. But the policy of this Government and of everybody in Canada is that we should not deal with countries that do not want to sign the non-proliferation treaty. We presume when a country signs non-proliferation treaty that that country will follow the treaty. If we presume a country has one type of government rather than another, that one will respect the treaty and that another country will not, there is no possibility of any international business, international negotiation and communication. If countries do not follow the treaty they will have to face the consequences mentioned in the treaty and world public opinion.
January 23, 1984

If someone says we should not sell them anything that is one thing. We had a debate in this House about the nuclear industry. I was not the Minister responsible at the time but I see the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) remembers that there was a very lively debate about how strict Canada should be about that business. Canada has more or less played a leading role in that sphere and in terms of non-proliferation. We should keep following that course. If though there are some suggestions to be made, we are willing to entertain them.
I have to come back to the first point and say that this topic has not been a major problem in the last 17 months. This is the first time either in the House or in committee that I am facing a debate on it. I guess the proposition of the Hon. Member for Regina East is typically an overkill. Members of the New Democratic Party do not look at reality. They just say turn the clock back 40 years and forget that nuclear energy has ever been developed. As the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey said, the genie is out of the bottle and we have to cope with it. We have to cope with it in a rational way.
There are some problems. I do not deny that. I think the disposal of tailings is always a problem. Safety is always a problem. I am personally preoccupied with some of the problems with which we have been faced in the last little while. Nobody wanted a spill. I am sure neither the industry nor the New Democratic Party government which gave the licence for the mine operation wanted to have a spill. When the plans were cemented for production to proceed in Key Lake, the AECB asked for the plans, looked at them and it was satisfied they were good enough. Apparently there was human error. However, we should not exaggerate and scare people too much because of the great quantity of polluted water that spilled. The spillage will be collected, reprocessed and there will be no permanent damage. We are working at this time with the provincial administration, the company and the federal agencies involved to make sure that the reprocessing of the spilled water will be reprocessed to protect the ecology.
We should not exaggerate. The quantity of uranium in that water is very small. I am told it is less than what you find naturally in some waters sometimes. But this is an unfortunate incident. We should not have spills of that nature. As long as there are humans working in plants, one cannot always have 100 per cent assurance on everything. Nevertheless, I think it can be managed.
The question is, should we or should we not have a nuclear industry in Canada and a Candu reactor in operation? This form of energy development was decided a long time ago. Canada invested a lot of money over the years to make sure that we would be at the forefront of the new technology when it started. Today nuclear energy is very important in many countries of the world. More than 50 per cent of France's electricity is produced or will be produced from nuclear sources. Finland, Sweden, Belgium and Switzerland depend on nuclear energy for more than 30 per cent of their energy requirements. Countries like Japan, Germany, the United States and the United Kingdom are more dependent upon
Supply
nuclear energy than Canada. One-third of the electricity produced in Ontario is produced from the nuclear industry. That percentage will rise. We are dealing with an industry that exists at this time and it accounts for 36,000 jobs today.
We are at the crossroads today and there is a very difficult decision to make. There was some slackening in energy demand because of conservation programs. Speaking of conservation programs, we spend half a billion dollars, more or less, on conservation programs of all sorts. The answer is not to go to solar energy. I do not think we will ever solve the energy problem in Canada through solar. We help that industry. There is a demand and there is a certain market for solar energy. But there are countries that benefit more than we do from solar energy. We have many more days in Canada when it rains than does Mexico, and there are many countries that have 250 days of sun a year that cannot use only solar energy. This form of energy is not necessarily the solution to all our problems.
There are other forms of energy that can be used. There has been reference to hydrogen. We are working on that. On Friday the National Research Council announced the opening of an electro-chemistry lab, the first one to be built at this time. It is being built in the St. Maurice Valley with the La Prade funds that were made available to that general area from the closing of the heavy water plant at La Prade. There was a fund established for a new form of energy and that money was used for the lab announced on Friday.
Is that in your riding?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Yes. It is logical. Electro-chemistry in Canada started in Shawinigan long before I was born. My father worked on the first dam and the first hydro-electric development in Canada in 1890-something in Shawinigan, where I was born. People in Shawinigan are quite happy with it.
I think we have to concentrate on finding a solution. The Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey asked some good questions. What should we do with atomic energy? Should we or should we not carry on? Should we sell more Candu reactors or not sell them any more? My approach is that we should try. Of course, we have some problems. The capital costs of the Candu reactors are higher than the American, the German or the French systems. Things are now getting more and more competitive. The operating costs of the Candu are much less than others. Of course, we would not sell to any country that does not want to sign the non-proliferation treaty. I have had some requests and I have said: "No. If you sign we can talk business but if you don't, we won't talk business". We have to make sure of that. If we only have the Canadian market and the demand at the level it is today, then the Hon. Member is right; the industry would shrink. That is why at this time we are in negotiation with other countries trying to sell our Candu reactor.

January 23, 1984
Supply
When we talk about human suffering, we can see that many countries need that type of energy if they want to develop. Because of the price of oil, and if they have no other resources, then the Candu reactor can be the key alternative to give many developing nations the energy they need. The policy of the Government is to try to sell Candu reactors so we can maintain a viable industry in Canada. In doing that we have to make sure of the safety of the operation. The incident that we had to deal with last summer in Ontario was pretty interesting.
I was terribly disappointed when the Pickering nuclear generating station had some problems, but it was kind of satisfying that those problems were solved in a very safe and easy way. We did not have to use any of the many devices that are in place for emergencies. When the trouble occurred it was realized that it could be managed on a calm basis rather than a crisis management basis. That is the proof of the safety of the system. Of course, we always have to make sure there is no danger. I think the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey must represent areas where there is some of that industry and he does not seem to be too frightened by it. If we do not get too scared about it, I think we can manage most of the problems.
I think all Members of the House who would like to debate this problem should make sure that there is a good discussion when the estimates come before us. I should like to receive the many ideas that can be put forward at that time. Tailings are a big problem. There is uranium in the ground already and the tailings have to be put where they will not create any problems.
Then what do we do about reprocessing spent fuel? Storage is a difficult and costly matter, but so far it has not created major problems for anyone. When we have to dispose of it permanently, we must make sure that it is done in a safe way. Money is being spent at this time to find a permanent solution to the disposition of spent fuel. There are those who claim that it might all virtually be reused and some experiments are being carried out at this time to make sure that it can be disposed of in a completely safe way.
On Indian lands.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The attitude of the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) is that there is some danger in this. However, people have put swimming pools on property next to the Pickering plant. You can swim there if you want, so that means it is not very dangerous. If you want to scare people and not look at the facts, however, you can always make a case and say: "You have virtually an atomic bomb in your backyard".
We must be responsible in this, Mr. Speaker. It is important for Canada. We already have uranium mining. Now that the government of the Party of the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) is no longer in power, he wants to close down the mine. But that Party in government gave permission for development of the mine. It cannot have it both ways. It cannot close down the industry as an example to the world and
say we will not have Candu reactors for sale because they are built with the technology and the industry of central Canada. Of course, we have to export the uranium produced in Saskatchewan. If we do not want to deal with uranium, then we should not deal with it at all. We should be completely logical and close the industry down altogether. I do not think a lot of people would want us to give up 36,000 jobs in Canada at this time.
There are some very positive aspects in this, Mr. Speaker. For example, there is the progress we have made through the technology developed in the field of medical research and even for medical services in terms of cobalt and other techniques. Because of the difficulties in the world now, we are less aggressive. We have even had to lay off some people lately because of lack of demand. Some good medical technology and medical instrumentation has been developed out of nuclear research and this has helped people who are sick. A lot of progress has been made so we should keep it but make sure there is no great danger.
I do not think a royal commission would solve the problem. It would be easy to appoint a royal commission and to say that since it will take about a year to report, do not ask me any questions. But I would rather be asked questions and then I will try to deal with the problem, Mr. Speaker. I do not think this problem calls for a royal commission, Mr. Speaker, but there is probably a need for more debate in the House. About 10 different commissions were created in Saskatchewan, Ontario and Quebec on the nuclear industry.
You will be over on this side a year from now.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The Hon. Member lives in an unreal world. The election is only a year from now, so he should keep having his illusions. What is important is the day of the election and we are usually pretty good that day!
I am not about to accept such a course, Mr. Speaker. It would be too easy for me to do that. I am not running away from the problems either. I think I have dealt with those that have been mentioned. The industry is facing some difficulties today.

It is not a growth industry at the present time, because conservation programs throughout the world have caused a drop in demand for energy, which, in fact, is a very good thing. However, in the long term I think Canada will do well to maintain a nuclear industry that was developed by Canadian scientists and produced CANDU, one of the best systems in the world. We want to sell the system to prospective buyers who are prepared to observe international rules on non-proliferation.
However, I am open to ideas and suggestions from all Members on the subject, so that we can prepare and make the necessary decisions with maximum input from the Members of this House.
January 23, 1984

I think the approach taken by the Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) was much more reasonable because it sought solutions and asked valid questions. The position taken by the Member for Regina-East (Mr. de Jong) was, unfortunately, a simplistic one. It urged complete withdrawal, dropping everything. We must realize there is no such thing as a simple answer to complex problems. I hope that today's debate will provide solutions and enable us to approach the problems in a non-partisan way, so that I myself, my departmental officials and Government agencies responsible for Atomic Energy will be able to take the necessary corrective action, and any valid suggestions will be most welcome, both to me and to my very dedicated and very able parliamentary secretary.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Comments and questions. The Hon. Member for Saskatoon-East.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister one question which has to do with the non-proliferation treaties. I understand that any country can get out of the non-proliferation treaties with a 90-day notice. I appreciate the fact that Canada has a more strict interpretation of that; however, I believe that much of the uranium which is now around the world has been sent out under a non-proliferation treaty and then in a parallel way has reached other countries. Does the Minister feel that Canada's involvement with this kind of distribution of uranium around the world is going to influence the credibility of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as he tries to find solutions to the question of world peace?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these are two different problems. We have a technology which is available to the countries who want to buy it and we are asking every nation of the world who wants to buy Canadian technology to sign a non-proliferation agreement. The Hon. Member's asking me for a legal opinion on how they can get out of this. I do not know exactly. I presume that the safeguards are such that they cannot get away easily from the agreement. There is also a monthly discussion being had in Vienna to improve on these situations. Many of the committees there involve people coming from Canada because our country is among the most determined to bring about an international solution to this problem.
In terms of will it help or not help the peace mission of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), I believe it is well known that we in Canada are unanimous in condemning nuclear weapons and we do not want to have them in Canada. We are not developing them here in Canada. I feel these are two different problems. Making available to the nations of the world the possibility of having energy in many of the countries which are not as advanced as we are has nothing to do with the making of bombs.
I believe the contribution of the Prime Minister has been supported by all Hon. Members of this House. I was very pleased with the kind of support which was given to him in Stockholm by the former Leader of the Opposition, the Right
Supply
Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark). I feel that is the type of approach we have. I do not believe it is very useful today to try to mix the two problems. We are talking today about a technology which has been developed in Canada which will produce electricity for the people who buy it. This has nothing to do with the making of the bomb because anyone who wants to use Canada's technology has to sign a non-proliferation treaty. I suppose it is our international contribution. There are many countries now who depend on nuclear reactors for more than 30 per cent of their electricity. I believe it is a bit ridiculous to try to forget about this reality.
Mr. Speaker, I have a very brief question for the Minister. Is there written down anywhere the policy of the Liberal Government in dealing with nuclear energy and the Candu reactor?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was a review made some years ago, I believe in 1980-81, and it was made public. I have not had a review since I became Minister. I have delivered some speeches but not many. I will tell the House at this time that our policy is yes, we want to carry on with the Candu reactor. We want to sell some Candu reactors abroad under conditions which I have previously expressed with respect to exporting electricity from Candu reactors built in Canada. There are public hearings now before the National Energy Board with respect to Lepreau, New Brunswick. One of the conditions I am committed to is that if the Candu reactor is being built, it has to be built without subsidy. It has to be built on its own. If the utility company in New Brunswick wish to build another reactor next to the one it has and sell the electricity, as long as it does not involve any subsidy from the federal Government and is done on a commercial basis, personally I have no objection. It must meet with the concerns of the local citizens and there will be some public hearings in terms of the environment and social impact and the people can express their views.
That is, in a nutshell, the policy which I am enunciating today. I believe it would be good to have a committee discuss the problem and I can be asked more specific questions. However, the policy remains the same as it was before, but it has been adjusted to the realities of today.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to inform the Minister that there was a parliamentary committee looking into this whole question, particularly that of nuclear waste disposal in Canada, some years ago, but it never had its terms of reference renewed by the Government. Therefore, that study was never completed by Parliament. The Minister might very well consider going back and looking at the terms of reference and setting it up again.
I would like to ask the Minister about the disposal of nuclear waste in Canada. He mentioned briefly some of the options which are being considered, and at one point he stated in his remarks that the option of the re-use of nuclear waste was being considered. I would like to know by whom it is being considered and whether or not it has been considered by the Government. Is it one of the options the Government itself is

January 23, 1984
Supply
placing some weight on? Does the Minister realize that this would take us into a whole new generation of nuclear reactors about which many people have very grave reservations?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am just saying that one of the alternatives which is being studied by the industry and AECL at this time is what to do with spent fuel. One of the options considered is that it might be reutilized. However, the question is can the technology be developed to do it on an economic basis. If it creates some side problems, which the Hon. Member seems to be alluding to, this aspect is being considered also. It is not something for today. I know that the spent fuel is being stored at this time near the site, either in Bruce or in Pickering or even in Lepreau. They have their pool and the spent fuel is put there. You can store a certain amount for a certain number of years, but what do you do in the long term? We do not know.
It is a problem which has an international preoccupation. I met not long ago with the Secretary General of the United Nations who deals with these problems in Vienna and it is one of the very difficult problems it would like to solve. It would like to have an international regime to dispose of all nuclear waste so that everyone will have the same standards and it will be completely secure.
Some might even argue that if you sell a Candu reactor to a country and you take back the spent fuel and the plutonium, it cannot then make bombs. I do not know if that is a solution, but it might be. If the preoccupation is that we do not trust so-and-so, we can take back the spent fuel and the plutonium. I am not an expert, but apparently one cannot make the bomb without it. So that might be a condition, I do not know. I am just throwing out an idea which has not been extensively debated. That is why I say I welcome a debate on this issue. I believe it is a good opportunity to do so today and I am sorry it did not happen sooner.

Mr. Speaker, we were all very interested in the remarks of the Minister. He seemed to fluctuate between saying yes, we need more debate and, on the other hand, closing the door to any need for a public inquiry. Surely the Minister agrees that there are technical question marks, especially in terms of tailings and nuclear waste. I believe the Minister will also agree that the economics of the nuclear industry are shaky. In fact, since 1975 there has been a net decrease of some 31,000 megawatts of plant capacity, and in the United States alone, since 1973 about 100 plants have been cancelled. I feel that Canada is at a crossroads: should it continue supporting the investment it has made in the nuclear industry, or should it cut its losses? Would the Minister not agree that this type of debate and these types of decisions should be made in an open forum, and would the Minister not reconsider the need for a public inquiry into the nuclear industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I do not believe we need an inquiry at this time. I have been Minister for 17 months. What I am saying is that some people have raised that problem. However, it did not become a problem which is not manageable. It is the first time
we are having a debate on it. I have been in committees of the House since I have been Minister and there have been very few questions; virtually no questions have been asked on that issue.
I feel that the decision has to be made by the House of Commons eventually. It would be a very easy answer for me to say we should have a royal commission and wash my hands of the problem. But we are faced with decisions today: should we sell or not sell to Turkey? A commission can give me the answer in two years but it is today that I have to make a decision. Should we sell another one to Korea?
The point I am making is that decisions have to be made today, not have a royal commission. I do not think we need a commission; we need the view of the House of Commons. I think we can make a responsible decision with the advice of Members of the House of Commons. Why always go outside? I think we can make our own decision here. That is my view.

Mr. Speaker, 1 say at the outset I particularly welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate on this motion dealing with a subject which I suggest is long overdue. The substance of the motion certainly justifies the consideration of this House here or in committee. I want to point out as well that the NDP does not have a monopoly on matters concerning the environment and nuclear issues. I well remember, and I am certain Members on my left will as well, the efforts of the 1979 Progressive Conservative Government when it attempted to establish a joint committee of Parliament to study a full and wide range of nuclear issues, perhaps wider than those which would be considered under the inquiry which is the subject of today's motion.
The issues proposed for consideration by that 1979 Conservative Government, Mr. Speaker, included the essence of today's motion as well as the whole question of where this nation should be headed with its nuclear energy program. The formation date of that joint committee was stalled from time to time by the joint efforts of the NDP and Liberal Party, until finally they worked together to overthrow that Conservative Government. That was the last time you heard of matters pertaining to nuclear energy in any great substance, Mr. Speaker, until this motion today.
It might be said, Mr. Speaker, that hindsight is simply wonderful, but I know the actions of the NDP in 1979 put off any real examination of these urgent and pressing matters over this period of time. That is what led to the comments of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin), when he, with his extensive knowledge and experience in matters pertaining to nuclear energy in this country, expressed surprise and delight that this subject matter is before us today for consideration.
Today, Mr. Speaker, the NDP is back in the House introducing a motion far weaker than the one they prevented from coming forward in 1979. Perhaps our thinking even in 1979 was far ahead of theirs in 1984. In 1979 we in the Progressive Conservative Party foresaw the problems and issues which
January 23, 1984

might develop from a nuclear energy program. I need only refer to Bill C-270 and Bill C-218 put forward by my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan) and the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey, to illustrate that particular point. Having said that, I have to admit to some reservations about today's motion. With the indulgence of this House I would like to devote a few moments to giving some background to the issue.
Many Members of this House are familiar with what was known as Bill C-14, the Nuclear Control and Administration Act, introduced in late 1977. That legislation died on the Order Paper and has not been reintroduced by this Government. Nonetheless, that legislation was a first step toward addressing the main problem with respect to uranium mining, the question of jurisdiction. Mining tends to fall in between federal and provincial areas of responsibility, and the federal Government has in fact delegated, sometimes by way of default, its responsibility for safety to the provinces. This is a deliberate attempt by this federal Government to shirk and avoid its responsibilities. It is also a constitutional question which must be addressed sooner or later, and it would have been in 1979 had it not been for the deliberate actions of the Government Party and the Party to my left.
The motion before us today does not make allowances for this. Far from it. The motion simply barges ahead on the assumption that this federal Government has the responsibility for everything and anything. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that a better starting point would have been to tackle the main issue of responsibility and resolve it first.
We then have to ask the question whether the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) is not both something too little, yet something too much. There is no lack of studies and material on the nuclear industry. The Porter Commission, for example, only recently completed its study for the Province of Ontario. Energy, Mines and Resources has just issued a discussion paper, "Nuclear Industry Review: Problems and Prospects of 1981-2000". All of the material points in one direction, the necessity for the formation of a parliamentary committee concerned with the energy needs of this country, the alternative forms of energy, sources and supply, and what really is in the best interests of this country.
The motion before us proposes a royal commission to concentrate primarily on uranium, only one aspect of this broad energy question. I suggest that if such a motion were adopted and a royal commission were established, it would take as its starting point the terms as outlined rather than the debate which takes place in this House today, and this nation would be all the poorer for that.
When we talk about something constructive, it is in recognition of the fact that Canada's nuclear industry needs a review. The industry is very much at a crossroads in that foreign orders for the Candu reactor are essentially non-existent. The domestic market is reaching a saturation point. These two considerations have led us to layoffs and to some real soul-searching about where this industry is going to go from here. It may well be that greater emphasis will have to be laid
Supply
on electricity exports. That is part of an ongoing parliamentary consideration. At present Canada is supplying only 1 per cent of the electricity requirements of the United States of America. Even so, this amounts to over $1 billion of import revenues to this country. Sales like this are certainly not above consideration; they are well worth pursuing. To do so it may be necessary for us to become even more competitive. We must be able to guarantee an uninterrupted supply of that form of energy. This clearly is not possible in an atmosphere where the nuclear industry is under attack and mothballed until sales of Candu reactors can be resumed. New directions and electricity export targets must be set out. After the kind of constructive review that we in this Party want to give it, it is worth bringing about.
I spoke earlier about Bill C-14 and I would like to return to that legislation. It illustrates why the motion before us today does not offer a full enough solution. It does not go far enough. Bill C-14 was designed to replace the Atomic Energy Control Act which was passed in 1946. The 1946 Act established the Atomic Energy Control Board and gave the Board jurisdiction throughout the entire country over the Canadian nuclear industry. A few regulatory amendments have been made since 1946. The basic Act remains as it was written in 1946 and is far outdated. Bill C-14 was the first attempt to revise that legislation. The legislation would have provided the necessary legislative and regulatory authority to meet the issues and anticipated concerns of the people of Canada and Members in this House.
Although the legislation died, it did have one single purpose: it did serve to underline the need for updating that 1946 Act. The nuclear industry has grown at a rapid rate since World War II. Yet this country has never had a full inquiry into whether this form of energy is in the best interest of the nation.
We in the Conservative Party have tried to do this more than once. My colleagues, the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) and the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan), as Private Members, have proposed that the nuclear regulatory process be made much more public and that Parliament be given a greater opportunity to participate in filling the energy needs of this country. Special mention should also be made of my colleague's proposal that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Caccia) be made Minister responsible for the administration of the Act. This is in full recognition of the fact that environmental concerns, including public health and safety, must be seen to be paramount in the nuclear cycle.
Bill C-270, last session, put forward by the Hon. Member for Hillsborough, was talked out on February 2, 1983. The Government speaker indicated a degree of support for the legislation but found it too hastily drafted. We could and might dispute that claim. Whether it is true or not, from that day on the Government has not brought forth any alternate legislation or opportunity for us to consider it further. We need

that opportunity to consider the shortcomings of the 1946 Atomic Energy Control Act. The Government has failed to make available to us the opportunity that is so needed.
That is why 1 welcome the opportunity to speak to this motion introduced by the NDP today. Many of the concerns raised by the motion of the Hon. Member for Skeena would and should be addressed in a new Bill. The remaining concerns should be met by a national inquiry conducted through a joint committee of this House of Commons rather than by way of a royal commission.
I urge the Government to table the necessary legislation and to establish such a parliamentary committee to review the nuclear industry in its entirety. Restricted as it would be by this motion, a royal commission would not provide the solution necessary. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to address this most important subject.

subtopic: CALL FOR REVIEW OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT PROGRAM
CALL FOR REVIEW OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Toronto Star reported on Sunday, January 22, that the program for enabling long term illegal but established migrants to become legal seems to be failing and even supporting a rip-off. While only 301 illegal migrants have been given a preliminary approval, 648 of them in Ontario alone have been ordered out of the country. That is over twice as many. No doubt some of those ordered out were short term, or failed to establish themselves, but the figures underline the way the program has turned sour since it was undertaken by the previous Minister of Employment and Immigration on June 29.
The majority of Canadians support the original policy, which was to encourage established immigrants to become legalized, where possible, by allowing them to apply anonymously at first. Unfortunately the present Minister has changed the policy. He introduced a rigid rule which excludes many migrants who may have been here for more than five years. He failed to enlist the help of knowledgeable individuals and non-profit community groups, as the Robinson Report advised, and he makes no serious attempt to publicize the program. Then he announced an early cut-off date when less than 2 per cent had even applied. As a result, we now find that panicky migrants are being ripped off by unscrupulous consultants for $1,000, $3,000, or even more, to make their applications.
I call on the Minister to review his program, remove the unnecessary restrictions, use reputable non-profit community organizations to assist these people to become good Canadians, and so end this rip-off of defenceless people.

subtopic: MEASURES NEEDED TO ASSIST ATLANTIC PROVINCES
MEASURES NEEDED TO ASSIST ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Atlantic provinces, with their resource-based and service-based economies, are traditionally the first hit, the hardest hit, and the last to recover from policies of tight money, restraint and austerity which the Government of Canada finds necessary to impose from time to time.
At the present time, with taxation at the highest level possible, the Atlantic provinces, which are 48 per cent dependent upon transfer payments from Ottawa, have incurred current account deficits of about three-quarters of a billion dollars despite severe restraint measures. To borrow to meet this deficit will have a detrimental effect upon credit ratings, interest rates, and marketability of bonds.
Measures similar to the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants of 1958 may be an urgent short-term solution, but the long-term answer is a secondary manufacturing base which
can expand the tax field and reduce dependence on the federal Government. It is essential for the Government of Canada to establish with the provinces common economic goals and objectives, and to invest in enlightened development policies which will have the positive dividend of establishing national standards for basic services and reducing economic dependence on the national Treasury.

subtopic: EFFECT OF CARBON BUILD-UP IN ATMOSPHERE
EFFECT OF CARBON BUILD-UP IN ATMOSPHERE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report of the U.S. Government Environmental Protection Agency of October, 1983, made official what many private scientists have been warning us about for years. The EPA warned that the build-up of carbon particles in the atmosphere will lead to the "greenhouse effect". They warned that the effect will begin to happen much sooner than first realized. Major changes will be here by the year 1990 to 2000, causing massive changes in climatic patterns throughout the world. Coastal areas will be flooded, while other areas like my home district of southern Saskatchewan will become deserts.
While scientists warn that the greenhouse effect is irreversible, they also state that the degree of climatic change will depend upon present and future policies. They all agree that we have to stop burning fossil fuels. There are solutions. Hydrogen is the cleanest burning fuel. It remits no carbon particles. The main recommendation of the parliamentary committee on alternate energies was that Canada move to a hydrogen economy. What is lacking is the political will and foresight.
The Government is spending billions of dollars in grants and subsidies on northern and offshore oil exploration, but hardly anything on alternate, safe, renewable energy forms. Is it not time that we wake up to what is happening? Is it not time that we had some leadership and foresight, rather than the policies we have now, based on short-sightedness, ignorance, and greed. The future of earth demands it.
